title: Awake Posterior Pharyngeal Wall Augmentation (Injection Pharyngoplasty) for Velopharyngeal Insufficiency
source_label: Operative Techniques in Laryngology (2024), Ch 63 Awake Posterior Pharyngeal Wall Augmentation for Velopharyngeal Insufficiency
indications: Awake injection augmentation of the posterior pharyngeal wall treats mild to moderate, partial or unilateral velopharyngeal insufficiency causing hypernasality, nasal regurgitation or dysphagia. It is particularly useful in adults with acquired VPI after stroke, cranial neuropathy, skull base or oropharyngeal cancer treatment, or radiation, who are poor candidates for a pharyngeal flap or sphincter pharyngoplasty. A temporary gel is a sensible trial for a new or possibly recovering deficit, and calcium hydroxylapatite is used for durable augmentation. Complete or bilateral palatal paralysis creates too large a gap for injection alone. Real-time endoscopic feedback during speech and swallowing is the main advantage of the awake technique.
setup: Patient seated upright in office, procedure room or OR; topical anesthesia with or without light sedation
Oxymetazoline and 4% plain lidocaine (50:50) spray and pledgets for both nasal passages
Flexible endoscope with working channel (preferred) or rigid 0- or 30-degree telescope, with suction available
Augmentation material: temporary hyaluronic acid or carboxymethylcellulose gel, or calcium hydroxylapatite for durable effect
Long 25-gauge needle bendable 30-45 degrees, curved Abraham cannula, tongue depressor or gauze for peroral access

Check for medialized internal carotid arteries before injecting: look for posterior wall pulsation on endoscopy and review CT or MR angiography when available, especially in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, where retropharyngeal carotids are common
landmarks: Middle meatus on the side of the VPI (best endoscopic window)
Velum and its closure pattern during speech and swallow
Passavant ridge on the posterior pharyngeal wall
Expected course of the internal carotid artery lateral and posterior to the injection sites
danger: Intravascular, especially carotid, injection at lateral sites, or at the midline when the carotids are medialized (22q11.2 deletion)
Deep injection into the prevertebral space
Overcorrection causing obstructive sleep apnea or hyponasality
Aspiration while the pharynx is anesthetized
steps: Select the patient

Inject for partial or unilateral VPI with hypernasality, nasal regurgitation or dysphagia, especially in adults after stroke, cancer resection or radiation who are poor candidates for a pharyngeal flap or sphincter pharyngoplasty. Complete or bilateral palatal weakness leaves too large a gap for injection alone.
Choose the material

For a new cause that may improve, trial a temporary hyaluronic acid or carboxymethylcellulose gel. For persistent VPI or after a good trial, use calcium hydroxylapatite, which lasts about 12 months and can be repeated. Fat is autologous but needs a large needle and usually general anesthesia, which loses awake feedback.
Setting

Perform the procedure under topical anesthesia, with or without light sedation, in the office, a procedure suite or the OR. Seat the patient upright. Awake feedback with speech and swallowing during the case is the main advantage over general anesthesia.
Prepare the nose

Examine both nostrils for septal deviation or turbinate hypertrophy. Spray and then place pledgets soaked in a 50:50 mix of oxymetazoline and 4% plain lidocaine, and allow several minutes before removing them.
Pass the endoscope
Pass a flexible scope (ideally with a working channel) or a rigid 0- or 30-degree telescope through the middle meatus on the side of the VPI for the most direct view.
Map the gap dynamically

Watch velopharyngeal closure during speech and swallowing to find the exact location and size of the gap and the target spot on the posterior wall. This precise mapping matters more than anything else.
Topicalize the target

Drip 4% plain lidocaine through the scope's working channel onto the planned injection site. Or apply it perorally by spray, atomizer or a curved Abraham cannula passed up into the nasopharynx just before the needle goes in.
Choose the route

Transnasally, the needle can go through either nostril. Perorally, rehearse the angle with a curved cannula and bend a long 25-gauge needle about 30-45 degrees. Depress the tongue or have the patient pull it forward with gauze to clear the tongue base.
Prevent intravascular injection

Before injecting, especially at lateral sites, draw back on the syringe and confirm there is no vascular flash. Carotid injection is rare but catastrophic, so plan each site with the vessel course in mind.
Inject at Passavant ridge

Under continuous endoscopic view, inject submucosally into the posterior pharyngeal wall at the level of Passavant ridge, right at or next to the mapped gap. Place the material as superficially as possible and inject slowly.
Use few sites

Inject through as few separate punctures as possible, because each extra site raises the risk that augmentation material extrudes. If the scope has a channel, use suction to clear secretions and any extruded material during the case.
Reassess and top up

Recheck velopharyngeal closure between injections and treat any persistent gap. Slight overinjection allows for some absorption. Bleeding at the needle entry is usually minimal and stops on its own without intervention.
Aftercare and follow-up

Keep the patient NPO for 2 hours until the topical anesthetic wears off, then resume the usual diet with over-the-counter analgesics. Warn that multifactorial dysphagia may persist. A rare prevertebral inflammatory reaction can last up to about 3 weeks. Reinject when benefit fades.
exit_check: Improved or complete velopharyngeal closure on endoscopy during speech and swallow
No extruded material or active bleeding at puncture sites
postop: NPO for 2 hours until topical anesthesia wears off, then usual diet
Counsel that multifactorial dysphagia may persist despite improved closure
Report fever, severe neck pain or stiffness, or worsening swallowing promptly
Reassess speech and swallow; reinject when effect fades (hydroxylapatite about 12 months)

early: Minor bleeding at the needle entry
Prevertebral inflammatory reaction or infection lasting up to about 3 weeks
late: Early absorption with loss of benefit
Obstructive sleep apnea or snoring from overaugmentation
Need for repeat injection or conversion to flap or sphincter pharyngoplasty

attending_followup: Which patients are best suited to posterior pharyngeal wall injection?
Mild to moderate, partial or unilateral VPI with a small mapped gap; large gaps from complete or bilateral palatal paralysis need a pharyngeal flap or sphincter pharyngoplasty.
Submucosally and superficially in the posterior pharyngeal wall at Passavant ridge, directly at or adjacent to the mapped gap.
Real-time endoscopic assessment of closure during speech and swallowing lets you target and titrate the injection precisely.
What catastrophic complication is guarded against, and how?
Intravascular carotid injection; plan sites with the vessel course in mind and draw back for a vascular flash before each injection.
Temporary gel for a trial or possibly recovering deficit; calcium hydroxylapatite for persistent VPI (about 12 months); fat is autologous but usually requires general anesthesia and a large needle.
